story: ABR, Inc., Fairbanks and Anchorage environmental research and consulting firm, already runs machine learning in production but does not say so anywhere a client looks first
drift_pattern: TWO directional patterns, both matter more than the individual errors. FIRST, a run of small errors ALL LEAN TOWARD MAKING ABR LOOK FURTHER BEHIND ON TECHNOLOGY THAN THE EVIDENCE SUPPORTS. The package asserted ABR has 'no drone or UAS program named on its site' when ABR's own Remote Sensing page lists 'aerial and UAV photography' in the same bullet list the package quoted from. Same direction: SWCA was quoted non-verbatim in a form reading more AI-forward than the actual sentence, and Stantec's unverifiable claims were carried at all. Strip those three and the honest competitive finding gets NARROWER AND STRONGER, not weaker. ABR does machine learning, its homepage says only 'leading edge technologies', and that is a POSITIONING gap not a CAPABILITY gap. DO NOT LET THE STUDY WIDEN IT BACK OUT. SECOND, precision drift in the industry section. Scale figures were carried at a precision the cited pages do not print (OWL-C '5 hours for 26 gigapixels', KAMERA '1.5 million image sets and 26 TB', every Ecobot number). The headline metrics on those same pages all verified. USE THE VERIFIED HEADLINE, NEVER THE UNVERIFIED SCALE DETAIL.

Authors' own limits: deployment-scale empty-terrain specificity remains future work, detection threshold was test-optimal not held-out validated. REPORT THOSE LIMITS IN THE SAME BREATH AS THE METRICS.

Naming him makes the finding narrower and more credible.

claims.claim: The PLoS One evaluation reported sensitivity of 0.88 to 0.97 for the common, acoustically distinct species, in a deliberate best-case test
claims.verbatim: While our analyses intentionally used high-quality, hand-picked echolocation calls by known species to provide a best-case scenario for automated classifiers, all three programs struggled with accuracy for some species, obtaining metrics well below what is advertised.
claims.notes: RE-FETCHED BY THE SHOWRUNNER 2026-07-30 after the study-critic flagged the first version of C60 as manufactured. IT WAS RIGHT AND THE FIGURE WAS ALSO WRONG. There is NO '96 to 99 percent' sentence in this paper. That string came from an unverified annotation in C46's notes. The real Table 1 sensitivities on common species are 0.88 to 0.97. The paper's own framing matters more than the numbers: the calls were hand-picked to give a BEST CASE, and all three still struggled for some species.
claims.value: Table 1 sensitivity: big brown bat KPro 0.88 SonoBat 0.90; tricolored bat KPro 0.91 SonoBat 0.97

claims.claim: MIT NANDA, as reported by Fortune, on buying versus building AI capability
claims.verbatim: Purchasing AI tools from specialized vendors and building partnerships succeed about 67% of the time, while internal builds succeed only one-third as often.
claims.notes: RE-FETCHED BY THE SHOWRUNNER 2026-07-30 because the study-critic asked whether the two-to-one split had been read or carried from recall. IT HAD NOT BEEN READ. And the MULTIPLE IS AMBIGUOUS in the source: 'internal builds succeed only one-third as often' reads literally as roughly three times, while the article's own gloss implies 67 vs 33 which is twice. knowledge/AI_SCOPING.md says 'about twice'. The study now prints the unambiguous 67 percent figure and avoids asserting a multiple. Also confirms the headline: 'About 5% of AI pilot programs achieve rapid revenue acceleration; the vast majority stall, delivering little to no measurable impact on P&L.' SECONDARY SOURCE, attribute to the reporting.
